title: Call on Me
hookLine: your Lord said, call on Me and I will answer (40:60)

cards: There's a kind of person who'd rather drive in circles for half an hour than stop and ask for directions. Or carry a heavy couch up three flights alone rather than text a neighbor.
Or sit with a problem for months rather than say the words: I need help. It's not that they can't ask. Something in them won't.
Back on day one hundred thirty, this path met du'a, the open, anytime prayer of asking. Today's verse comes at it from the other side: the person who won't ask.

teach.b: Surah Ghafir, verse sixty. Pickthall: "And your Lord hath said: Pray unto me and I will hear your prayer. Lo! those who scorn My service, they will enter hell, disgraced."
The first half is an invitation and a promise: ud'uni, call on Me, astajib lakum, I will answer you.

teach.h: THE WARNING IS FOR THE PROUD.
teach.b: The second is a warning, and here's the surprise: it isn't aimed at people who ask for the wrong things. It's aimed at those too proud.
The Arabic is yastakbiruna, from kibr, the same pride the Qur'an names when Iblis refused to bow. Too proud for what? 'an 'ibadati, for My worship.
The verse begins with asking and ends with worship, as if they were the same thing. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ read it that way.
In Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, he says du'a is worship, and recites this very verse.
So, in this verse, not asking isn't a sign of strength. It can be pride. A hadith in al-Tirmidhi puts it sharply: whoever doesn't ask Allah, Allah is displeased with him.
People tire of being asked; in this hadith, it's the not-asking that displeases. When someone asks, they admit they need, and the hadith counts that asking as worship.
So the verse turns the couch-carrying instinct upside down. Asking isn't weakness to be avoided. It's the invitation.

how: Muslims make du'a at any time and in any language, often raising their hands, and especially after prayers, in the last third of the night, and between the call to prayer and its start.

o: remember Me, a call to say God's names
call on Me, God's invitation to ask Him
obey Me, a command to follow the law

games.q: call on Me — tap the pairs.

s: the warning in 40:60 is for people who ask for the wrong things
it's for those too proud to call on Him.
the Prophet recited 40:60 after saying du'a is worship
reported in Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi.
a hadith says Allah is displeased with those who don't ask Him

games.q: you've carried a problem alone for months. you could ask God, and others, for help. what does 40:60 say about not asking?
o: it's a sign of strong faith.
it can be a kind of pride.
games.why: the verse warns those too proud for His worship, and the Prophet read asking as worship itself.

practice: Notice one thing you've been carrying alone, too proud or too tired to ask for help with.

If you pray, ask Allah for it now, plainly, in your own words, and let go of how the answer will come; if you don't, name the need out loud to yourself, and think of one person you could ask. Either way, sit with the asking done.

wordCard.voice: Ud'uni, call on Me, Ghafir sixty's invitation and promise, paired with a warning for those too proud to ask. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: call on Me, I will answer you (40:60).

carryVoice: Your line: call, and be answered. In this verse, the asking is itself worship. Day five hundred sixty-three, done.
